title: Anxiety, Fear & Avoidance
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

nodes.title: Start here
nodes.body:
Your body's alarm system can activate before you have worked out what is happening. We need to understand the signal before deciding how much authority to give it.

What is a bodily alarm telling us, and how do our responses affect the next one?
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), cognitive model of panic; NICE CG113 anxiety and panic guidance.

nodes.title: What alarm response means
nodes.body:
A set of bodily changes that prepares us to respond to possible threat.

For example: Heart rate rises and breathing becomes faster before a crowded lecture.

One important limit: A familiar anxiety response is not automatically dangerous; new or severe symptoms still deserve appropriate assessment.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), cognitive model of panic; NICE CG113 anxiety and panic guidance.

nodes.title: Find the first concept
nodes.prompt: Consider this example: Heart rate rises and breathing becomes faster before a crowded lecture. Which concept is most directly demonstrated, without claiming anything beyond the example?
nodes.explanation: The example most directly supports alarm response. A set of bodily changes that prepares us to respond to possible threat. A familiar anxiety response is not automatically dangerous; new or severe symptoms still deserve appropriate assessment.
nodes.counterexample: A strong bodily response is not itself proof of either safety or danger. Clinical assessment and context matter, especially for unfamiliar or severe symptoms.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), cognitive model of panic; NICE CG113 anxiety and panic guidance.

nodes.title: What threat appraisal means
nodes.body:
The mind's estimate of what could go wrong and how likely or costly it might be.

For example: A racing heart is interpreted as proof of an imminent collapse.

One important limit: An appraisal can be compelling without being accurate.

nodes.title: What avoidance means
nodes.body:
Staying away from a feared situation or leaving it to reduce distress.

For example: Someone steps out of a room each time their heart begins to race.

One important limit: Leaving can be reasonable when danger is real; its effects differ when the threat is only anticipated.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), cognitive model of panic; NICE CG113 anxiety and panic guidance.

nodes.title: What exposure means
nodes.body:
Approaching a safe feared situation sufficiently to learn what happens without relying on escape.

For example: Someone gradually stays through a familiar anxiety surge and observes it change.

One important limit: Exposure should be planned around real safety and a person's circumstances, not forced regardless of risk.

lessons.title: First notice what happened
lessons.teach: Read what is said before deciding why anyone said it.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Ava is about to enter a crowded lecture theatre. Her heart is pounding. Tom is waiting beside her.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), cognitive model of panic; NICE CG113 anxiety and panic guidance.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: A strong bodily response is not itself proof of either safety or danger. Clinical assessment and context matter, especially for unfamiliar or severe symptoms.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), cognitive model of panic; NICE CG113 anxiety and panic guidance.
nodes.scenario: Ava is about to enter a crowded lecture theatre. Her heart is pounding. Tom is waiting beside her.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: My heart's racing. Something feels wrong.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Are you having any new symptoms that need medical attention?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: No, it's the familiar surge I get before crowded rooms.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What usually happens if you leave straight away?

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. A strong bodily response is not itself proof of either safety or danger. Clinical assessment and context matter, especially for unfamiliar or severe symptoms.
checks.counterexample: A strong bodily response is not itself proof of either safety or danger. Clinical assessment and context matter, especially for unfamiliar or severe symptoms.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: A strong bodily response is not itself proof of either safety or danger. Clinical assessment and context matter, especially for unfamiliar or severe symptoms.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), cognitive model of panic; NICE CG113 anxiety and panic guidance.

items.label: “My heart's racing. Something feels wrong.”
The bodily alarm may be interpreted as evidence of danger. Escaping brings rapid relief, which can reinforce future avoidance even when the anticipated harm remains untested.
“Are you having any new symptoms that need medical attention?”
Ava could be reacting to a genuine problem in that environment, or to symptoms that require medical assessment rather than exposure.

nodes.body:

lessons.title: Two explanations can sound reasonable
lessons.teach: Evidence should be able to change which explanation you prefer.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
The bodily alarm may be interpreted as evidence of danger. Escaping brings rapid relief, which can reinforce future avoidance even when the anticipated harm remains untested.

Another possibility: Ava could be reacting to a genuine problem in that environment, or to symptoms that require medical assessment rather than exposure.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), cognitive model of panic; NICE CG113 anxiety and panic guidance.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Compare anticipated outcomes with what happens when the situation is approached safely, with appropriate medical safeguards. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: A strong bodily response is not itself proof of either safety or danger. Clinical assessment and context matter, especially for unfamiliar or severe symptoms.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), cognitive model of panic; NICE CG113 anxiety and panic guidance.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Compare anticipated outcomes with what happens when the situation is approached safely, with appropriate medical safeguards.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: On three previous occasions Ava stayed in the room despite a similar familiar surge; the sensations peaked and then reduced without the feared collapse.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), cognitive model of panic; NICE CG113 anxiety and panic guidance.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: Those experiences weaken the prediction that the familiar sensations necessarily lead to collapse and give her evidence about tolerating them.
nodes.counterexample: A strong bodily response is not itself proof of either safety or danger. Clinical assessment and context matter, especially for unfamiliar or severe symptoms.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), cognitive model of panic; NICE CG113 anxiety and panic guidance.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: The feeling isn't the forecast

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), A Cognitive Approach to Panic; NICE CG113.
nodes.scenario: Iris notices her heart racing while waiting for a crowded train.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: My heart just started beating really fast.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Are you feeling faint or having any other worrying symptoms?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I'm afraid I'm going to collapse in front of everyone.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Would you like to sit somewhere quieter while we decide what to do?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Now I'm checking every beat. It feels faster when I focus on it.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: We should check actual risk without treating the sensation alone as a prediction.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Iris may be interpreting bodily arousal as evidence of imminent danger.
A physical cause for the racing heart needs medical attention.
The crowd's noise or proximity may be overwhelming without fear of collapse.
Ava could be reacting to a genuine problem in that environment, or to symptoms that require medical assessment rather than exposure.
options.feedback: This is a plausible competing hypothesis. Its relative strength depends on whether it accounts for the most revealing details.

options.label: The bodily alarm may be interpreted as evidence of danger. Escaping brings rapid relief, which can reinforce future avoidance even when the anticipated harm remains untested.
options.feedback: A process formulation may fit, but the evidence may also support other contributors.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Iris may be interpreting bodily arousal as evidence of imminent danger. A physical cause for the racing heart needs medical attention. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: New, severe or concerning physical symptoms warrant appropriate medical assessment. A psychological explanation must not substitute for evaluating physical risk.

checks.prompt: You are Iris. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

options.label: Before making any decision, I'd like you to explain exactly why you responded that way.
options.reply: Would you like to sit somewhere quieter while we decide what to do?
options.consequence: Demanding a definitive motive may provoke another defence rather than settle the issue.

options.label: Let's ask someone else to intervene before discussing this further.
options.consequence: Independent help can be appropriate when direct discussion fails or safety requires it; timing matters.

options.label: First check for concerning symptoms; if safe, distinguish what is happening in the body from what you fear will follow.
options.reply: That tells us something about attention, not the cause of the heartbeat.
options.consequence: The conversation may not be solved, but the immediate problem now has a concrete route forward.

options.label: Leave every crowded place as soon as your pulse changes.
options.reply: We should check actual risk without treating the sensation alone as a prediction.
options.consequence: Backing away can ease pressure now while leaving the original concern unresolved.

options.label: Ava could be reacting to a genuine problem in that environment, or to symptoms that require medical assessment rather than exposure.

nodes.explanation: Escalation can be proportionate when a direct attempt has failed. Its safety and usefulness depend on the situation. A strong bodily response is not itself proof of either safety or danger. Clinical assessment and context matter, especially for unfamiliar or severe symptoms.

options.feedback: Reassurance can help but cannot guarantee action on a concrete problem.

options.label: Force yourself to remain inside regardless of any symptom changes.
options.feedback: This makes the unresolved issue reviewable without needing to diagnose the other person.

options.label: A previous disagreement may have shaped the response, making the present conversation part of a longer pattern.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
Someone experiences a familiar racing pulse before a presentation and avoids the room, later concluding that avoiding it prevented a disaster.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
The bodily alarm may be interpreted as evidence of danger. Escaping brings rapid relief, which can reinforce future avoidance even when the anticipated harm remains untested.

A strong bodily response is not itself proof of either safety or danger. Clinical assessment and context matter, especially for unfamiliar or severe symptoms.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: Clark (1986), cognitive model of panic; NICE CG113 anxiety and panic guidance.

glossary.definition: A set of bodily changes that prepares us to respond to possible threat.
glossary.example: Heart rate rises and breathing becomes faster before a crowded lecture.
glossary.limit: A familiar anxiety response is not automatically dangerous; new or severe symptoms still deserve appropriate assessment.

glossary.definition: The mind's estimate of what could go wrong and how likely or costly it might be.
glossary.example: A racing heart is interpreted as proof of an imminent collapse.
glossary.limit: An appraisal can be compelling without being accurate.

glossary.definition: Staying away from a feared situation or leaving it to reduce distress.
glossary.example: Someone steps out of a room each time their heart begins to race.
glossary.limit: Leaving can be reasonable when danger is real; its effects differ when the threat is only anticipated.

glossary.definition: Approaching a safe feared situation sufficiently to learn what happens without relying on escape.
glossary.example: Someone gradually stays through a familiar anxiety surge and observes it change.
glossary.limit: Exposure should be planned around real safety and a person's circumstances, not forced regardless of risk.
